screens.title: Lists and Sets — Managing Ordered and Unique Collections
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll explore two foundational Redis collection types: Lists and Sets. Lists are ordered sequences implemented as linked lists, giving you constant-time additions and removals at the head or tail. That makes them ideal for feeds, message queues, or any scenario where new items arrive and old items are processed. Sets, by contrast, enforce uniqueness and do not preserve order. They excel at tracking membership, tags, or unique visitors, and they support very fast union, intersection, and difference operations used in analytics and recommendation logic. You will see how core commands behave, learn performance considerations, and practice common patterns like trimming lists to a fixed size and using blocking pops for worker queues. We’ll also highlight common mistakes, for example requesting entire large lists without pagination. By the end you will understand when to choose a List versus a Set, how to operate them safely in production, and simple recipes you can apply immediately, such as maintaining a recent activity feed or finding users who share interests. Ready to try practical commands and real examples that map directly to these use cases?

screens.title: Redis Lists — ordered sequences and linked-list behavior
screens.narratorSegment: A Redis List is an ordered collection of strings implemented internally as a linked list. That implementation detail gives us a key guarantee: pushing or popping from the head or tail is a constant-time operation. In practice this means LPUSH and RPUSH add items instantly at either end, and LPOP and RPOP remove items instantly from either end, regardless of the list length. Why does that matter? Because lists are the right choice when you need an ordered stream of items where new entries are frequently placed at one end and older entries are processed at the other — think message queues, activity feeds, or simple stacks. A common pattern is to LPUSH new events and RPOP to consume the oldest event. One misconception is assuming lists are like arrays with random access similar in cost; LRANGE or fetching an arbitrary index is linear in the number of elements returned, and moving through a long range can be costly. A concrete example: use LPUSH to add a new feed item for a user and use LRANGE 0 9 to show the ten most recent items. Key takeaway: favor Lists for ordered streams with head/tail operations, and avoid using them when you need frequent random-access reads of very large ranges. How would you model a producer/consumer pipeline using these guarantees?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Redis Lists — definition
What is a Redis List?

An ordered collection of strings implemented as a linked list, making head and tail operations extremely fast.

Complexity Profile
  • LPUSH / RPUSH and LPOP / RPOP are O(1) — constant time regardless of list size.
  • LRANGE is O(N) where N is number of elements returned; retrieving very large ranges can be costly.
  • LLEN is O(1) to get list length, LREM is O(N) relative to elements scanned.
Key Takeaway

Use Lists when you need ordered streams with frequent head or tail changes; avoid LRANGE on entire massive lists.

Common misconception

Lists are not arrays optimized for random access. Pulling large ranges is linear in the output size and can impact performance.

Concrete example
LPUSH user:alice:feed "post:102 Alice liked a photo"
LPUSH user:alice:feed "post:101 Alice shared an article"
LRANGE user:alice:feed 0 4  -- show five most recent posts
RPOP user:alice:feed        -- process oldest post
Explanation bullets
  • LPUSH inserts at the head; the newest items appear first when you LRANGE from zero.
  • RPOP removes the tail, which is useful to process oldest items in FIFO producer/consumer patterns.
  • Combine LRANGE with LTRIM to show recent entries while keeping list size bounded.
Try this

Simulate a producer with LPUSH and a consumer with RPOP; observe constant-time behavior as the list grows.

screens.title: Head and Tail Operations — LPUSH, RPUSH, LPOP, RPOP
screens.narratorSegment: Head and tail operations are the workhorses of Redis Lists. LPUSH adds one or more elements to the left side, and RPUSH adds to the right side. Correspondingly, LPOP removes and returns the leftmost element and RPOP removes and returns the rightmost. These operations are constant-time, which makes them perfect for producer/consumer patterns. Consider a queue where new tasks are LPUSHed and workers use BRPOP to wait for tasks at the tail; the oldest tasks are processed first, implementing FIFO behavior. A common alternative is using RPUSH and LPOP to the same effect; the choice simply mirrors your intended convention for head versus tail. One pitfall is expecting list methods to reorder elements arbitrarily — Lists preserve the sequence of pushes and pops. A concrete example: to implement a stack, RPUSH and RPOP form LIFO behavior; to implement a queue, LPUSH and RPOP implement FIFO. Try to articulate which pair you would pick for a delayed task scheduler and why. Remember that combining these operations with trimming or blocking pops yields robust production patterns. Head and Tail Operations — LPUSH, RPUSH, LPOP, RPOP means lpush/rpush and lpop/rpop are constant-time primitives; combine them to build fifo queues or lifo stacks and use blocking variants for consumers.. In practical terms, how to add and remove items reliably for queues and stacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Process
keyIdea.text: LPUSH/RPUSH and LPOP/RPOP are constant-time primitives; combine them to build FIFO queues or LIFO stacks and use blocking variants for consumers.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › LPUSH / RPOP Patterns
Common pairs and their semantics
  • LPUSH + RPOP — newest inserted at head, oldest removed from tail, FIFO queue.
  • RPUSH + RPOP — add to tail, remove from tail, LIFO stack if used together.
  • RPUSH + LPOP — alternate convention to get FIFO depending on your push side choice.
Process example
LPUSH tasks "task:cleanup:1"
LPUSH tasks "task:send_email:2"
RPOP tasks  -- consumer processes the oldest task
Pro tip

Choose one convention across producers and consumers to avoid confusion. Document whether head is newest or oldest.

Common mistake

Mixing conventions between services can invert FIFO/LIFO expectations and cause subtle bugs.

Example scenario

Background workers should use blocking pops for efficiency. The producer pushes work and the consumer blocks waiting for items, avoiding busy polling.

Why it matters
Blocking pops reduce CPU usage and latency for event-driven workers. They allow reliable handoff between producers and consumers without tight loops.
Key Takeaway

Map push/pop pairs to the behavior you need — FIFO or LIFO — and keep producers and consumers consistent to avoid logic errors.

screens.title: Retrieving and Trimming — LRANGE, LLEN, LREM, LTRIM
screens.narratorSegment: Reading and maintaining lists requires two complementary skills: retrieving slices efficiently and keeping lists bounded. LRANGE returns a contiguous range of elements but its cost is proportional to how many elements you request. For small windows, such as the ten most recent feed items, LRANGE is fine. However, calling LRANGE zero minus one to get everything on a very large list can be expensive and should be avoided. Use LLEN to check size and LTRIM to keep only the most recent N items; LTRIM is an efficient server-side operation that truncates the list without transferring unnecessary items over the network. To remove occurrences of a specific value, use LREM which scans the list and removes matching elements; this is linear work relative to the list length. A concrete CLI demonstration: fetch the five most recent posts with LRANGE key 0 4, then ensure the list does not grow unbounded by running LTRIM key 0 99 after LPUSH operations. Misconception to watch: trimming and range retrieval are different actions — LRANGE reads items, LTRIM mutates the stored list. Which pattern would you adopt to show recent activity while limiting memory growth?

keyIdea.text: Use LRANGE for small windows, LLEN to check size, and LTRIM to keep lists bounded. Avoid LRANGE 0 -1 on huge lists.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › LRANGE & LTRIM Demo
Common retrieval and maintenance commands
  • LRANGE key start stop — returns a slice; cost proportional to number of elements returned.
  • LLEN key — returns the length in O(1).
  • LTRIM key start stop — truncates list server-side to the specified range; useful for bounding history.
  • LREM key count element — removes occurrences and is O(N) with respect to list length.
CLI snippets
LRANGE user:alice:feed 0 4   -- show five most recent
LLEN user:alice:feed           -- get current feed length
LTRIM user:alice:feed 0 99     -- keep recent 100 items
Common mistake

Using LRANGE 0 -1 on a very large list moves many elements over the network and can block your application; paginate or trim instead.

Example scenario

For a feed UI request the most recent page only, and maintain the list size on write using LTRIM after each LPUSH so the server never retains unnecessary history.

Key Takeaway

Read small windows with LRANGE and use LTRIM to bound list growth. Treat LREM as a heavier operation that scans for matches.

Pro tip

Apply LTRIM right after LPUSH to keep storage predictable: push then trim is an efficient pattern.

screens.title: Blocking Operations — BLPOP and BRPOP for reliable workers
screens.narratorSegment: Blocking operations let a client wait for an element to appear instead of polling. BLPOP and BRPOP are blocking variants of LPOP and RPOP. If the list is empty, the blocking call waits until an element is available or until a timeout elapses. This is exceptionally useful for worker processes that should sit idle with minimal C P U cost until work arrives. A typical pattern has producers LPUSHing tasks and workers calling BLPOP with a timeout to claim a task as soon as it is pushed. An important caveat is to choose an appropriate timeout: zero specifies infinite waiting, which is convenient but requires robust handling in your worker logic. A snippet demonstrates opening two CLI windows: one blocks waiting on a named list and the other pushes a task; the blocking client returns immediately with the new item. Misconception to avoid: blocking pops do not permanently hold a connection; they simply keep the client waiting. Key takeaway: use BLPOP/BRPOP to implement efficient, reliable, and low-C P U worker queues. Blocking Operations — BLPOP and BRPOP for reliable workers means blpop and brpop let consumers wait for tasks, eliminating busy-polling and lowering cpu usage for background workers.. In practical terms, how blocking pops avoid polling and reduce cpu usage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Blocking Pops
Behavior and benefits
  • BLPOP and BRPOP block until an element is available or the timeout expires.
  • They remove and return the element, making them ideal for handing off work to one consumer atomically.
  • Blocking reduces polling and CPU usage compared to tight loops checking list length.
CLI demonstration
# Window 1: consumer blocks
BLPOP user:bob:tasks 10

# Window 2: producer pushes a task
LPUSH user:bob:tasks "task:clean_cache"
Note

Use an appropriate timeout value to let your application handle reconnects or shutdowns gracefully. Zero means wait forever.

Example scenario

A transient worker can call BLPOP with a reasonable timeout in a loop. On receiving a task it processes and continues waiting. On timeout it can check for shutdown signals or re-register.

Key Takeaway

Blocking pops are a low-overhead way to implement producer/consumer patterns; use them rather than polling to conserve CPU and simplify coordination.

screens.title: Redis Sets — unordered unique collections
screens.narratorSegment: Redis Sets are unordered collections of unique strings. Uniqueness is enforced automatically: adding the same member multiple times has no effect beyond the initial insertion. Because Sets do not maintain order, they are not appropriate when the sequence matters; instead they are ideal for membership and deduplication tasks, such as tracking unique visitors, storing tags for articles, or recording users who liked a post. Sets are powerful because they support fast set algebra: you can compute unions, intersections, and differences across multiple sets with commands like SUNION, SINTER, and SDIFF. This makes them excellent for queries that combine or compare categories, for example finding users interested in both sports and news. A common misuse is treating Sets as if they preserve order or relying on SMEMBERS to fetch very large sets without using scanning; for large sets prefer SSCAN to iterate without blocking the server. Concrete example: add users to a tag's product set and use SINTER to find users who have both tags. What query would you run to find items unique to one tag versus another? Redis Sets — unordered unique collections means sets provide unique, unordered storage and support very fast union, intersection, and difference operations for membership queries and analytics.. In practical terms, how sets differ from lists and when to use them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Redis Sets — definition
What is a Redis Set?

An unordered collection of unique strings. Duplicates are rejected automatically and order is not preserved.

When to use Sets
  • Track unique visitors or likers for a resource.
  • Maintain tags for articles and compute related items via intersections.
  • Create inverted indices like tag to product ID mappings for fast filtering.
Common mistake

Do not depend on Sets for order. If you require a ranking or sorted ordering, use a Sorted Set instead.

Concrete example
SADD article:1:tags "redis" "database" "cache"
SADD article:2:tags "redis" "performance"
SISMEMBER article:2:tags "cache"   -- checks membership
SCARD article:1:tags                -- cardinality of the set
Key Takeaway

Use Sets when uniqueness matters and set operations can express your queries more simply and efficiently than scanning other structures.

SMEMBERS returns all members, but for very large sets you should prefer SSCAN to iterate without blocking. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Set Commands
Essential set commands
  • SADD key member [member ...] — add unique members.
  • SMEMBERS key — return all members; avoid on huge sets.
  • SISMEMBER key member — check membership fast.
  • SREM key member [member ...] — remove members.
  • SCARD key — return the unique member count.
CLI snippets
SADD article:1:tags "redis" "database" "cache"
SMEMBERS article:1:tags
SISMEMBER article:2:tags "cache"
SCARD article:1:tags
Best practices
  • Use SSCAN for large sets to iterate incrementally and avoid blocking the server.
  • Keep inverted indices for frequent multi-tag queries: tag:name -> set of item IDs.
  • Use SREM to maintain accuracy when items are deleted or untagged.
Common misconception

Treating SMEMBERS as always safe. It is convenient for small sets, but assume SSCAN or paged access for large production collections.

screens.title: Set Operations — SUNION, SINTER, SDIFF and STORE variants
screens.narratorSegment: Set algebra is where Redis Sets really shine. SUNION computes all members present in any of the input sets — useful to find users interested in either of two topics. SINTER returns only members present in all input sets, enabling queries like users who like both sports and news. SDIFF returns members that are in the first set but not in subsequent ones, which lets you detect exclusive interests. Each of these commands has a STORE variant that writes the result into a new key, which is efficient for caching computed results for later queries. A practical pattern is maintaining tag-to-product inverted sets and then using SINTER to produce a candidate list for multi-tag searches. A common misconception is expecting set operations to maintain order — they do not. Also, while set operations are fast, materializing very large union results without storing can produce heavy network traffic. Think about whether to compute a result on demand or precompute it into a stored set for repeated use. Which operation would you pick to find users who are in both 'sports' and 'news' groups?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Set Operations
Operation semantics
  • SUNION set1 set2 ... — union of members across sets.
  • SINTER set1 set2 ... — intersection: members present in every set.
  • SDIFF set1 set2 ... — difference: members in set1 not in others.
  • SUNIONSTORE, SINTERSTORE, SDIFFSTORE — compute and persist results in a new key.
Examples
SINTER tag:sports:users tag:news:users   -- users who like both
SUNION tag:news:users tag:tech:users        -- combined user set
SDIFF tag:action:users tag:horror:users     -- action but not horror
SINTERSTORE result:key tag:a tag:b         -- store the intersection
Practical notes
  • Use STORE variants when results will be reused to avoid repeated computation.
  • Set operations can combine many sets quickly, but materializing huge results may be costly over the network.
  • Design inverted indices for frequent queries so you can run intersections on small candidate sets.
Key Takeaway

Set algebra expresses complex membership queries compactly and performs well; choose between on-demand compute and stored results based on reuse and size.

screens.title: Lists vs Sets — choose the right type
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between a List and a Set is about two core requirements: ordering and uniqueness. If the sequence of elements matters and you need fast head or tail operations, choose a List. If you only care about whether an element exists in a collection and you need automatic deduplication or set algebra, choose a Set. A frequent production error is using a Set when the order matters — this leads to surprises in user interfaces. Conversely, using a List when you only need uniqueness forces you to manage duplicates manually, adding complexity. Consider performance implications: LPUSH and RPOP are constant time, while LRANGE and LREM can be linear in the number of elements returned or scanned. For Sets, SMEMBERS returns all members and can be heavy for big sets; SSCAN avoids blocking. A practical pattern is hybrid: store a user's feed as a List but maintain a Set of processed item IDs to prevent duplicates across services. Reflect on your current project: do you need ordering or uniqueness first? content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Lists vs Sets
Decision checklist
  • Do you need deterministic order? If yes, Lists.
  • Do you require uniqueness and set operations? If yes, Sets.
  • Will you perform frequent range reads of a long sequence? Consider pagination and trimming.
Hybrid pattern

Use a List for ordering plus a Set to deduplicate or index processed IDs. This gives both efficient order and uniqueness safeguards.

Pitfalls
  • Fetching entire large Lists with LRANGE can be expensive; paginate.
  • Using SMEMBERS on very large Sets can block; prefer SSCAN.
  • Misaligned push/pop conventions across services cause order bugs.
Reflective question

Which of your features needs order and which needs uniqueness? Could a hybrid approach simplify implementation?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll explore two foundational Redis collection types: Lists and Sets. Lists are ordered sequences implemented as linked lists, giving you constant-time additions and removals at the head or tail. That makes them ideal for feeds, message queues, or any scenario where new items arrive and old items are processed. Sets, by contrast, enforce uniqueness and do not preserve order. They excel at tracking membership, tags, or unique visitors, and they support very fast union, intersection, and difference operations used in analytics and recommendation logic. You will see how core commands behave, learn performance considerations, and practice common patterns like trimming lists to a fixed size and using blocking pops for worker queues. We’ll also highlight common mistakes, for example requesting entire large lists without pagination. By the end you will understand when to choose a List versus a Set, how to operate them safely in production, and simple recipes you can apply immediately, such as maintaining a recent activity feed or finding users who share interests. Ready to try practical commands and real examples that map directly to these use cases?

Over the next screens you will learn to distinguish Redis Lists from Sets, apply list operations to build queues and feeds, and manage unique membership with sets. First, you'll identify when an ordered sequence is preferred and why Lists implement head and tail operations with constant time cost. Second, you'll perform essential List commands to add, remove, and inspect items, and you will learn blocking operations for efficient worker queues. Third, you'll manage Sets: adding members, checking membership, retrieving counts, and applying union, intersection, and difference to answer real queries. Finally, we'll explore performance characteristics and common mistakes, such as retrieving entire large lists or misusing sets when order matters. Each objective includes a small mnemonic to help memory and a milestone label indicating verified competency. Work through the examples and the hands-on activity to practice these skills in a terminal demo style. By the end you will not only know commands but also be able to choose the right structure for a given problem and avoid common performance pitfalls.

This screen expands the practice goals and ties them to observable actions. You will run commands that add and remove items, paginate results, and use blocking pops to wait for work. For Sets, you will add members, check membership, and perform union and intersection to answer queries like finding users who share interests. Each objective includes a short mnemonic to help you remember the pattern and a verified milestone so you can self-check. Practically, you will complete a short terminal activity where you simulate a user's feed with LPUSH and process items with RPOP or BLPOP, then manage article tags using SADD and SINTER to find related content. Along the way we will point out how to avoid common mistakes like using LRANGE to fetch an entire huge list, or using Sets when order matters. These practice objectives aim to make your learning concrete so you can reproduce the patterns in your own projects after the lesson.

A Redis List is an ordered collection of strings implemented internally as a linked list. That implementation detail gives us a key guarantee: pushing or popping from the head or tail is a constant-time operation. In practice this means LPUSH and RPUSH add items instantly at either end, and LPOP and RPOP remove items instantly from either end, regardless of the list length. Why does that matter? Because lists are the right choice when you need an ordered stream of items where new entries are frequently placed at one end and older entries are processed at the other — think message queues, activity feeds, or simple stacks. A common pattern is to LPUSH new events and RPOP to consume the oldest event. One misconception is assuming lists are like arrays with random access similar in cost; LRANGE or fetching an arbitrary index is linear in the number of elements returned, and moving through a long range can be costly. A concrete example: use LPUSH to add a new feed item for a user and use LRANGE 0 9 to show the ten most recent items. Key takeaway: favor Lists for ordered streams with head/tail operations, and avoid using them when you need frequent random-access reads of very large ranges. How would you model a producer/consumer pipeline using these guarantees?

Head and tail operations are the workhorses of Redis Lists. LPUSH adds one or more elements to the left side, and RPUSH adds to the right side. Correspondingly, LPOP removes and returns the leftmost element and RPOP removes and returns the rightmost. These operations are constant-time, which makes them perfect for producer/consumer patterns. Consider a queue where new tasks are LPUSHed and workers use BRPOP to wait for tasks at the tail; the oldest tasks are processed first, implementing FIFO behavior. A common alternative is using RPUSH and LPOP to the same effect; the choice simply mirrors your intended convention for head versus tail. One pitfall is expecting list methods to reorder elements arbitrarily — Lists preserve the sequence of pushes and pops. A concrete example: to implement a stack, RPUSH and RPOP form LIFO behavior; to implement a queue, LPUSH and RPOP implement FIFO. Try to articulate which pair you would pick for a delayed task scheduler and why. Remember that combining these operations with trimming or blocking pops yields robust production patterns. Head and Tail Operations — LPUSH, RPUSH, LPOP, RPOP means lpush/rpush and lpop/rpop are constant-time primitives; combine them to build fifo queues or lifo stacks and use blocking variants for consumers.. In practical terms, how to add and remove items reliably for queues and stacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Reading and maintaining lists requires two complementary skills: retrieving slices efficiently and keeping lists bounded. LRANGE returns a contiguous range of elements but its cost is proportional to how many elements you request. For small windows, such as the ten most recent feed items, LRANGE is fine. However, calling LRANGE zero minus one to get everything on a very large list can be expensive and should be avoided. Use LLEN to check size and LTRIM to keep only the most recent N items; LTRIM is an efficient server-side operation that truncates the list without transferring unnecessary items over the network. To remove occurrences of a specific value, use LREM which scans the list and removes matching elements; this is linear work relative to the list length. A concrete CLI demonstration: fetch the five most recent posts with LRANGE key 0 4, then ensure the list does not grow unbounded by running LTRIM key 0 99 after LPUSH operations. Misconception to watch: trimming and range retrieval are different actions — LRANGE reads items, LTRIM mutates the stored list. Which pattern would you adopt to show recent activity while limiting memory growth?

Blocking operations let a client wait for an element to appear instead of polling. BLPOP and BRPOP are blocking variants of LPOP and RPOP. If the list is empty, the blocking call waits until an element is available or until a timeout elapses. This is exceptionally useful for worker processes that should sit idle with minimal C P U cost until work arrives. A typical pattern has producers LPUSHing tasks and workers calling BLPOP with a timeout to claim a task as soon as it is pushed. Redis Sets are unordered collections of unique strings. Uniqueness is enforced automatically: adding the same member multiple times has no effect beyond the initial insertion. Because Sets do not maintain order, they are not appropriate when the sequence matters; instead they are ideal for membership and deduplication tasks, such as tracking unique visitors, storing tags for articles, or recording users who liked a post. Sets are powerful because they support fast set algebra: you can compute unions, intersections, and differences across multiple sets with commands like SUNION, SINTER, and SDIFF. This makes them excellent for queries that combine or compare categories, for example finding users interested in both sports and news. A common misuse is treating Sets as if they preserve order or relying on SMEMBERS to fetch very large sets without using scanning; for large sets prefer SSCAN to iterate without blocking the server. Set algebra is where Redis Sets really shine. SUNION computes all members present in any of the input sets — useful to find users interested in either of two topics. SINTER returns only members present in all input sets, enabling queries like users who like both sports and news. SDIFF returns members that are in the first set but not in subsequent ones, which lets you detect exclusive interests. Each of these commands has a STORE variant that writes the result into a new key, which is efficient for caching computed results for later queries. A practical pattern is maintaining tag-to-product inverted sets and then using SINTER to produce a candidate list for multi-tag searches. Choosing between a List and a Set is about two core requirements: ordering and uniqueness. If the sequence of elements matters and you need fast head or tail operations, choose a List. If you only care about whether an element exists in a collection and you need automatic deduplication or set algebra, choose a Set. A frequent production error is using a Set when the order matters — this leads to surprises in user interfaces. Conversely, using a List when you only need uniqueness forces you to manage duplicates manually, adding complexity. Consider performance implications: LPUSH and RPOP are constant time, while LRANGE and LREM can be linear in the number of elements returned or scanned. For Sets, SMEMBERS returns all members and can be heavy for big sets; SSCAN avoids blocking. Let’s summarize the essentials. First, Redis Lists are ordered linked lists giving constant-time head and tail operations; use them for queues, stacks, and feeds.
